The map's label for early farming peoples of lowland South America who grew manioc (cassava), shown from 1500 BCE to 100 BCE.

Manioc is a root crop first bred in south-western Amazonia, on the southern edge of the basin in what is now Brazil and Bolivia, perhaps 8,000 to 10,000 years ago. It grows in poor soils and can be left in the ground until needed. Bitter kinds contain poison, so people learned to grate, soak, squeeze and toast the roots into flour and flatbread.

It spread across Amazonia, the Orinoco basin and the Caribbean, and became the staple food of the Tupi, the Taíno and many Amazon peoples. Farmers cleared small forest gardens, and over time their waste and charcoal built up dark, fertile terra preta soils.

After 1500 the Portuguese carried manioc across the Atlantic, and it reached Central Africa, where it became one of the continent's main foods.
